summary.text: Potential energy is the energy an object or system has because of its position relative to other objects, or the arrangement of its parts.
Common types are gravitational energy, the elastic energy of a deformed spring, and the electric energy of a charge in a field.
It is stored when an outside force works against a restoring force such as gravity, and it can be released when that force is let go.

items.prompt: You carry a box up the stairs and leave it on a high shelf. What has happened to the effort you put in?

options.label: It is stored in the force field as potential energy
It is gone, since the box is no longer moving
It is stored as heat in the shelf
It is now kinetic energy of the box

items.explain: Lifting a mass is done against the force field, and the work is stored in that field as potential energy.

items.prompt: You release a stretched spring and it snaps back. Why does it return?

options.label: The spring slowly makes more energy as it rests
The force field does work to move it back to where it began
Springs always move toward the warmest place
The stretch is permanently removed once held

items.explain: If the external force is removed, the force field acts on the body to move it back to its initial position.

items.prompt: Two hikers climb the same mountain, one by a steep trail and one by a long winding trail. How does gravity's total work compare?

options.label: The winding trail involves much more
The steep trail involves much more
The two are the same, as it depends only on the endpoints
It cannot be compared across different trails

items.explain: For conservative forces like gravity, the total work depends only on the initial and final positions.

items.prompt: One student says a book on a shelf has zero potential energy; another says it has plenty. How can both be right?

options.label: One of them must have weighed the book wrongly
Books only gain energy when they are opened
Energy is zero or large depending on mood
It is measured against a chosen reference position

items.explain: Potential energy is the difference between an object's energy at a given position and at a reference position.

items.prompt: A tank of gasoline is said to hold potential energy. What is that energy rooted in?

options.label: The motion of the tank inside the car
The arrangement of electrons and nuclei in its molecules
The weight of the liquid pressing down
The heat the engine will make later

items.explain: Chemical potential energy is the work of the Coulomb force during rearrangement of electrons and nuclei in atoms and molecules.

items.prompt: A hot gas's thermal energy has two parts. What are they?

options.label: Its color and the smell it has
Its volume and the pressure on it
Random particle motion and particle arrangement
Its container and the contents inside

items.explain: Thermal energy has two components: kinetic energy of random motions and potential energy of configuration.

paragraphs.heading: Energy stored by position
paragraphs.text: Potential energy is energy that an object or system has because of where it sits relative to other objects, or because of how its particles are arranged. It equals the work done against restoring forces, such as gravity or the pull of a spring. Common kinds include the gravitational kind, the elastic kind found in a deformed spring, and the electric kind held by a charge sitting in an electric field. In SI units it is measured in joules, written J.

paragraphs.heading: How it gets stored
paragraphs.text: When you stretch a spring or lift a mass, an outside force does work against the force field. That work is held in the field, and we call it stored potential energy. Take the outside force away and the field does the work itself, moving the body back where it started. The spring shortens, or the mass falls.

paragraphs.heading: A dropped ball
paragraphs.text: Picture a ball of mass m dropped from a height h. The free-fall acceleration g is roughly constant, so the ball's weight, mg, is constant too. Multiplying that force by the distance gives the work, which equals the gravitational potential energy: U_g = mgh. More formally, potential energy is the difference between an object's energy at a given position and its energy at a chosen reference position.

paragraphs.heading: Conservative forces
paragraphs.text: Potential energy belongs with forces whose total work on a body depends only on where the body starts and ends, not on the route between. Forces like this are called conservative forces, and gravity and spring forces are examples. The work a conservative force does is W = −ΔU, where ΔU is the change in potential energy. The minus sign is a convention: work done against the field raises potential energy, and work done by the field lowers it.

paragraphs.heading: One kind for each force
paragraphs.text: Each type of potential energy goes with a particular force. Elastic forces give elastic potential energy, gravity gives gravitational potential energy, the Coulomb force gives electric potential energy, and the forces between molecules give intermolecular potential energy. Chemical potential energy, like the energy in fossil fuels, comes from work done by the Coulomb force when the electrons and nuclei of atoms and molecules shift into new arrangements. Thermal energy usually has two parts: the kinetic energy of particles moving at random, and the potential energy of how they are arranged.

paragraphs.heading: Naming it
paragraphs.text: William Rankine, a Scottish engineer and physicist, coined the term potential energy in 1853 as part of a deliberate push to develop new terms. He chose it as half of the pair actual and potential, a contrast that goes back to Aristotle. In 1867 he described potential energy as energy of configuration and actual energy as energy of activity. That same year William Thomson brought in kinetic energy as the opposite of potential energy, and once his view was widely accepted, the term actual energy slowly fell out of use.
